reference.source: Valvular heart disease guidelines / cardiology references
clinicalPearls: Backflow across the tricuspid valve, most commonly functional (secondary) from right ventricular or annular dilatation rather than primary valve disease
Primary causes include endocarditis, rheumatic disease, Ebstein anomaly, carcinoid and device leads
Signs include a raised jugular venous pressure with a prominent v wave, a pansystolic murmur that increases on inspiration, pulsatile hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema
It is frequently associated with left-sided heart disease and pulmonary hypertension
Severe chronic regurgitation leads to right heart failure and hepatic congestion
Management addresses the underlying cause and pulmonary hypertension, with valve repair or replacement in selected severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Tricuspid regurgitation most often arises secondarily when right ventricular pressure or volume overload, commonly from left heart disease or pulmonary hypertension, dilates the right ventricle and tricuspid annulus so the leaflets fail to coapt. Primary (structural) regurgitation results from direct valve damage. The regurgitant volume overloads the right atrium and ventricle, raising systemic venous pressure to cause hepatic congestion, ascites and peripheral oedema, and chronic overload progressively impairs right ventricular function.
additionalDifferentials: Right heart failure of other cause
Mitral valve disease with secondary effects
Hepatic disease causing oedema and ascites
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography grading severity and assessing the right ventricle and annulus
Evaluation for left-sided valve or myocardial disease
Assessment for primary causes (endocarditis, carcinoid, leads)
Right heart and hepatic assessment in chronic disease
redFlags: Progressive right heart failure with congestion and ascites
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the underlying cause and right ventricular function; significant secondary regurgitation is associated with worse outcomes, and intervention decisions are individualised.
pitfalls: Overlooking treatable left-sided or pulmonary causes of functional regurgitation
Attributing congestion and ascites to liver disease alone
Delaying intervention until right ventricular function is severely impaired
Missing endocarditis or carcinoid as a primary cause
management: Treat the underlying driver of functional regurgitation by managing left-sided heart disease and lowering pulmonary artery pressure with pulmonary hypertension therapy where indicated
Relieve systemic venous congestion, hepatic congestion and oedema with loop diuretics, adding an aldosterone antagonist as needed
Provide rate or rhythm control and anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation contributing to atrial and annular remodelling
Address primary valve causes directly, with antimicrobials for endocarditis and management of carcinoid or lead-related regurgitation

Offer surgical tricuspid annuloplasty or valve replacement in selected severe cases, particularly at the time of left-sided valve surgery, and consider transcatheter tricuspid repair for high-risk patients
Perform serial echocardiographic surveillance of severity and right ventricular function, watching for progression to right heart failure
Manage decisions through a multidisciplinary heart valve team
